hints: For each solution list the ions present including $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ from water, then remember cations go to the cathode and anions go to the anode.
Recall the discharge rules: a reactive metal ion stays in solution so hydrogen is discharged, while a less reactive metal ion like $\text{Ag}^+$ or $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is discharged.
For the anode, think about when $\text{OH}^-$ gives $\text{O}_2$ versus when a concentrated halide gives $\text{Cl}_2$.
walkthrough:
Sort out who goes where**
Picture the cell. Negative ions are attracted to the positive anode where they lose electrons, positive ions are attracted to the negative cathode where they gain electrons. In aqueous solutions you always have $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ from water competing with the ions from the salt.

Decide the cathode products**
At the cathode the choice is between the metal ion and $\text{H}^+$. $\text{Ag}^+$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ are below hydrogen in reactivity, so they discharge easily to give $\text{Ag}$ and $\text{Cu}$ metal. $\text{Na}^+$ is very reactive and stays in solution, so $\text{H}^+$ from water discharges to give $\text{H}_2$.

Decide the anode products**
At the anode the choice is between the anion and $\text{OH}^-$. $\text{NO}_3^-$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ are very stable and stay in solution, so $\text{OH}^-$ discharges to give $\text{O}_2$. In concentrated $\text{NaCl(aq)}$, the high concentration of $\text{Cl}^-$ allows $\text{Cl}^-$ to discharge to give $\text{Cl}_2$.

Final answer: $\text{AgNO}_3\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_2$, cathode $\text{Ag}$
concentrated $\text{NaCl(aq)}$: anode $\text{Cl}_2$, cathode $\text{H}_2$
$\text{CuSO}_4\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_2$, cathode $\text{Cu}$

hints: Identify the only two ions present in molten $\text{CaI}_2$ and decide which moves to the anode and which moves to the cathode.
Remember oxidation is loss of electrons at the anode and reduction is gain of electrons at the cathode, then balance charge with $\text{e}^-$.
walkthrough:
See what is in the melt**
Molten $\text{CaI}_2$ contains only $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{I}^-$, no water is involved. $\text{I}^-$ moves to the positive anode, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ moves to the negative cathode. Inert electrodes just conduct electrons and take no part.

Write the two half equations**
At the anode, iodide loses electrons to form iodine molecules: $$2\text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2\text{e}^-$$ At the cathode, calcium ions gain electrons to form calcium metal: $$\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Ca}$$ Check that atoms and charges balance on each side.

hints: Link each half equation from (b)(i) to oxidation or reduction by deciding whether electrons are lost or gained.
Assign the oxidation number of Ca and I in the ions and in the elements, then track increase for oxidation and decrease for reduction.
walkthrough:
Spot reduction and oxidation together**
$\text{Ca}^{2+}$ gains electrons, that is reduction to $\text{Ca}$. $\text{I}^-$ loses electrons, that is oxidation to $\text{I}_2$. Because reduction and oxidation happen at the same time in the same cell, the overall electrolysis is redox.

Prove it with oxidation numbers**
Oxidation numbers give a clear bookkeeping check. For calcium: $$+2 \rightarrow 0$$ a decrease, so reduction. For iodine: $$-1 \rightarrow 0$$ an increase, so oxidation. One species reduced and the other oxidised confirms redox.

Final answer: Calcium is reduced and iodine is oxidised.
Oxidation number of Ca decreases from +2 in $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to 0 in $\text{Ca}$.
Oxidation number of I increases from -1 in $\text{I}^-$ to 0 in $\text{I}_2$.

hints: Visualise the products from (b)(i): what does solid calcium look like and what colour is iodine vapour, plus what happens to the volume of melt as it is converted?
walkthrough:
Translate products into what you would see**
Think with your eyes. At the cathode a grey or silvery metal coats the electrode as liquid or solid $\text{Ca}$ forms. At the anode you see characteristic purple vapour or fumes as $\text{I}_2$ escapes. Because $\text{CaI}_2$ is being consumed, the amount of melt steadily decreases.
Final answer: Any two: grey / silvery metallic deposit of Ca at cathode; purple vapour / fumes of $\text{I}_2$ at anode; amount of melt decreases.

hints: Start from $Q = It$, convert the time of 2 hours into seconds and calculate total charge, then convert to moles of electrons using $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.
Calculate moles of Fe deposited from mass $1.11\ \text{g}$ using $A_r = 55.8$.
Compare moles of electrons to moles of Fe to find electrons gained per $\text{Fe}^{n+}$ ion, which equals the oxidation number.
walkthrough:
Find how many electrons were supplied**
Charge links current and time: $$Q = It$$ Time must be in seconds: $$t = 2 \times 60 \times 60 = 7200\ \text{s}$$ So: $$Q = 0.8 \times 7200 = 5760\ \text{C}$$ One mole of electrons carries $96500\ \text{C}$, so: $$n(\text{e}^-) = \frac{5760}{96500} = 0.0597\ \text{mol}$$

Find how many moles of iron formed**
Use mass over molar mass: $$n(\text{Fe}) = \frac{m}{A_r} = \frac{1.11}{55.8} = 0.0199\ \text{mol}$$ Keep extra figures for the next ratio.

Use the ratio to get the ion charge**
Each $\text{Fe}^{n+} + n\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}$, so $n$ equals moles of electrons per mole of Fe: $$n = \frac{0.0597}{0.0199} = 3$$ Three moles of electrons deposit one mole of Fe, so the ion was $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and the oxidation number of Fe is +3.

Final answer: $$Q = It = 0.8 \times 2 \times 60 \times 60 = 5760\ \text{C}$$
$$n(\text{e}^-) = 5760 / 96500 = 0.0597\ \text{mol}$$
$$n(\text{Fe}) = 1.11 / 55.8 = 0.0199\ \text{mol}$$
$$n(\text{e}^-) / n(\text{Fe}) = 0.0597 / 0.0199 = 3$$
Oxidation number of Fe = +3
